longForm.title: The Battle of Hamburger Hill: Terrain, Attrition, and the Decision That Would Not Be Revisited
longForm.excerpt: In May 1969, the 101st Airborne Division made ten assaults on Hill 937 in the A Shau Valley. The hill was abandoned sixteen days after it was taken. The battle did not expose a tactical failure. It exposed an operational logic that had been running at cost for four years.
paragraphs: Hill 937 sits in the western end of the A Shau Valley, approximately two kilometers from the Laotian border. The terrain matters before anything else does. The hill rises steeply from the valley floor, triple-canopy jungle covering the upper slopes, with a series of ridgelines and draws that channel movement and give the defender observation of every approach. The 29th NVA Regiment had been using the A Shau Valley as a logistical corridor and staging area since at least 1966. By May 1969 they were occupying Hill 937 in strength, with a prepared bunker complex dug into the ridgelines and reinforced with overhead cover. Operation Apache Snow, launched by the 101st Airborne Division on May 10, 1969, was designed to clear the valley. Finding the hill occupied was not the plan. Finding it occupied by a regiment in prepared positions was a different problem still.

The initial contact on May 10 was made by 3rd Battalion, 187th Infantry — the Rakkasans — commanded by Lieutenant Colonel Weldon Honeycutt. Helicopter insertion into the valley placed the battalion at the hill's base. The first probe up the slope ran into automatic weapons and rocket-propelled grenade fire from positions that had been invisible from the air. One platoon took significant casualties before it could withdraw to defensible ground. The intelligence picture had underestimated both the size of the NVA force on the hill and the depth of their prepared positions. What the 101st Airborne had assumed was a screening force turned out to be a dug-in regiment with interlocking fields of fire, prepared fallback positions, and a logistics tail connected to Laos less than two kilometers away. Honeycutt reported the contact and requested support. The decision to assault the hill directly — rather than fix it in place and maneuver around it — was the central tactical choice of the battle, and it was not revisited for ten days.

The ground dictated the problem. The approaches to Hill 937's crest were narrow and dominated by the NVA positions above. Flanking maneuver required moving through jungle terrain that degraded unit cohesion and eliminated the fire superiority that the 101st depended upon. Air support — tactical strikes and B-52 Arc Light missions — hit the hill repeatedly but did not suppress the bunker complex. The bunkers were designed to survive. The NVA had dug into the reverse slope of each ridgeline, so that strikes hitting the forward slope detonated above and behind them. The hill had to be taken by infantry moving uphill through the bunker complex, and the NVA knew it. Between May 10 and May 19, the Rakkasans conducted nine assaults. Each time the leading elements got within reach of the crest, NVA fire from flanking positions drove them back. Each assault produced casualties. The terrain that made the hill tactically significant — observation over the valley — also made it extremely difficult to take.

Honeycutt's tactical situation was constrained in several directions simultaneously. He had one battalion on the objective, with additional battalions — 1st Battalion 506th and 2nd Battalion 506th Infantry — available to maneuver against the flanks and seal the NVA's escape routes. The broader Operation Apache Snow concept was working: NVA units trying to move away from the hill through the valley were intercepted. But the hill itself absorbed the fight. Honeycutt continued assaulting because every pause gave the NVA time to reinforce and repair, and because the tactical geometry of the position — its height, its prepared defenses, its connection to Laos — meant that leaving it in NVA hands left the valley operation incomplete. His commander, Major General John Wright, did not order him to break off. The assault continued. By May 18, with nine failed attacks behind them and casualties mounting, the Rakkasans had earned a name from the meat-grinder logic of the operation: Hamburger Hill.

The final assault went in on May 20, 1969, with four battalions converging on the hill simultaneously from multiple directions. The 3/187 attacked from the northeast, the 1/506 from the south, the 2/506 and 1/501 securing the flanks and blocking routes. The NVA had been reinforcing the hill through the Laotian connection throughout the battle — an avenue that the operational design had not fully closed. The assault on May 20 pushed through the bunker complex under fire. By midmorning the summit was in American hands. The NVA withdrew to the west, toward the Laotian border and the positions they would use to reoccupy the hill later. American casualties for the ten-day operation were 70 killed and 372 wounded. The 29th NVA Regiment lost an estimated 630 killed, along with equipment and prepared positions representing months of construction. The hill was held briefly. It was abandoned on June 5, 1969.

The political response was immediate. Senator Edward Kennedy took the Senate floor on May 20 — the day of the final assault — to denounce the battle as senseless and irresponsible, questioning the operational logic of assaulting a prepared position for ten days and then abandoning the objective within two weeks. The Washington Post and other papers picked up the critique. General Creighton Abrams, who had replaced Westmoreland as MACV commander, defended the operation on the grounds that it had destroyed a regiment and disrupted NVA logistics in the valley. Both assessments were accurate as far as they went. The regiment was significantly degraded. The NVA was back on the hill within the month. The debate in the Senate and the press was not really about Hill 937. It was about the operational logic of hill-clearing operations in general — about whether taking a position at significant cost, then abandoning it, was a coherent use of American combat power.

The abandonment of Hamburger Hill on June 5 became the symbolic moment that crystallized the critique of attrition warfare in Vietnam. The tactical argument for the abandonment was straightforward: the hill had no permanent value once the NVA regiment was destroyed, and holding it permanently would require continuous supply by helicopter under fire from Laotian-based artillery. The operational argument was harder to make. If the hill had no permanent value, the question of whether it was worth seventy American lives and three hundred and seventy-two wounded depended entirely on the weight one assigned to degrading the 29th NVA Regiment. That calculation required a theory of how attrition produced political results — a theory that MACV had been applying for years and that had not produced results proportional to the cost. Hamburger Hill did not create that critique. It gave it a specific geography and a body count.

The operational lesson that Hamburger Hill demonstrated, and that the subsequent debate partly obscured, was specific: direct assault on prepared hilltop positions along the Laotian border produced high casualties and temporary results because the NVA could reinforce and re-occupy from Laos faster than ARVN or US forces could seal the border. The tactical problem was real. The operational design — repeated direct assaults on fortified high ground connected to an unsealable sanctuary — was the mismatch. Abrams, to his credit, shifted the emphasis of US operations after Hamburger Hill toward pacification and away from the large-scale search-and-destroy sweeps that Westmoreland had favored. The shift came four years into a war that had been fought largely on the attrition logic that Hamburger Hill exposed. The NVA was back on Hill 937 before the end of June.

shortForm.title: Weldon Honeycutt and the Command Decision at Hamburger Hill
shortForm.excerpt: Lieutenant Colonel Weldon Honeycutt made nine assaults on Hill 937 before his battalion took it. The debate that followed conflated his tactical decisions with the operational commanders' strategic choices. They are not the same question.
paragraphs: Lieutenant Colonel Weldon Honeycutt made the decision to keep assaulting Hill 937 nine times before his unit took it on the tenth attempt. The decision has been criticized as inflexible, characterized in some accounts as a personal stubbornness that cost lives unnecessarily. The operational record does not entirely support that reading. Honeycutt's constraint was real: he was fighting a regiment in prepared positions on ground that offered no workable flanking option. The jungle terrain degraded unit cohesion on any approach that was not directly up the ridgeline. Flanking the hill would have required moving companies through thick vegetation with no aerial observation, against NVA forces who knew the ground and had secondary positions prepared. Fixing the NVA on the hill and maneuvering around it was the textbook option; in the terrain of the A Shau Valley in May 1969, it was not achievable at the platoon and company level.

The question Honeycutt faced was not whether to bypass — the terrain did not offer that option — but whether to continue direct assault or accept a tactical pause. Each pause gave the NVA time to reinforce through the Laotian connection and repair the bunker complex. B-52 Arc Light strikes on the hill between assaults produced significant blast damage and NVA casualties, but did not suppress the defended positions long enough for infantry to reach the crest before NVA survivors reoccupied firing positions. Honeycutt's professional judgment was that continuous pressure — maintaining contact and forcing the NVA to fight in place — was preferable to a pause that would be exploited. That judgment was defensible given the tactical geometry. Whether the broader operational decision to take the hill at all, given that it would be abandoned within two weeks, was worth the cost is a different question — one that rests with Major General Wright and above, not with the battalion commander on the ridge.

The debate that followed Hamburger Hill conflated the battalion commander's tactical decisions with the operational commanders' strategic choices. Honeycutt ran the assault as a professional. The question of whether the hill should have been assaulted at all — given the sanctuary problem, the temporary-objective logic, and the cost-to-benefit calculus of attrition warfare in 1969 — was not Honeycutt's to answer. He was given an objective. He took it. The critique that belongs at the battalion level is narrow: whether nine separate frontal assaults, with a tactical pause after each setback for consolidation and re-planning, might have produced a different result at lower cost. The more significant critique belongs one and two levels higher, where the decision to fight the 29th NVA Regiment on its prepared ground, in a valley connected to an unsealable sanctuary, was made and not revisited.

onThisDay.headline: British Forces Complete the Encirclement of Charleston
onThisDay.body: On May 4, 1780, British forces under General Henry Clinton completed the encirclement of Charleston, South Carolina, crossing the Cooper River and sealing the last American escape route. Major General Benjamin Lincoln's garrison of approximately 5,500 Continental soldiers surrendered on May 12, 1780, in the largest American defeat of the Revolutionary War.
